hub.description: Decks and fences for Brentwood, TN homes on sloped, wooded lots, planned around HOA review, rock, and hillside footings. Request an estimate.
hub.intro: Many Brentwood backyards are larger than a typical suburban lot, and plenty of them slope away from the house. A home that looks level from the street can drop a full story in back, down toward a line of hardwoods. On that kind of lot, a deck off the kitchen ends up well above the lawn, and a fence has to step or tilt its way down the hill. Many established subdivisions here also have an architectural committee that wants to see plans before anything gets built. Below is what to sort out before a deck or fence goes up on a Brentwood lot.

sections.heading: What a Brentwood lot asks of a builder
paragraphs: Start with the grade. On a hillside lot, the back of the house often sits well above the yard, especially over a walkout basement. That height shapes a deck from the footings to the stairs. It shapes a fence too, because panels have to follow the ground without leaving open gaps under the bottom rail. Anyone pricing a Brentwood project should walk the slope before talking about boards and colors, since the grade decides what is practical.

Trees come next. Many Brentwood neighborhoods were built into wooded hills, so a back property line often runs through mature hardwoods. Below the topsoil, limestone can sit closer to the surface than you might expect, and the clay above it holds water after a storm. None of this rules out a project. It means post holes and footings get planned around rock and roots from the start, instead of found halfway through the job.

sections.heading: Raised decks for hillside homes
paragraphs: On a sloped Brentwood lot, a deck built off the main floor is usually a raised deck, and sometimes a tall one. Tall decks need solid bracing so they do not sway. The ledger that ties the deck to the house has to be flashed and fastened with care. Stairs from that height run long, so a landing or a second, lower level often fits the slope better than one straight flight.

The space under a raised deck is worth planning too. Whether you live in Brentmeade or on a newer street, that area can become a shaded patio outside a walkout, or it can be closed in with skirting that still lets air through. Our [Brentwood deck builder page](/deck-builder-brentwood-tn/) goes further into footings in rock and the finish details that local committees and buyers notice.

sections.heading: Fences that follow the hill
paragraphs: Fencing a large Brentwood yard starts with deciding how much of it to fence. The back corners of a big wooded lot are often steep and deeply shaded, and hardly anyone walks them. A privacy fence out there is costly to build and easy to forget until a limb lands on it. Plenty of owners choose to enclose only the level stretch of lawn behind the house, where the dog and the kids actually spend their time.

Where a fence does cross a slope, the panels are either stepped, with each section level and dropping at the post, or racked to follow the ground. Gates need care on a hill so they swing clear. Property lines on wooded lots are often hard to see, so a survey or pinned corners come first. The [Brentwood fence installation page](/fence-company-brentwood-tn/) covers each of these in more depth.

sections.heading: HOA review and permits in Brentwood
paragraphs: Architectural review is common in Brentwood subdivisions, and committees usually care about how a project looks from the street and from the yards next door. For a fence, the questions are usually about style and height. Deck reviews tend to focus on placement and whether the stain suits the house. Approval normally comes before any building, and it is separate from a permit. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) explains how to put together a clean submission.

Permits are a separate question. Raised decks and decks attached to the house usually need one, while fence rules vary more from place to place. A Brentwood mailing address does not always mean the City of Brentwood handles your permit, because some of those addresses sit across the county line in Davidson County. Confirm which codes office covers your lot before anyone starts digging.

sections.heading: Getting a useful estimate in Brentwood
paragraphs: A good first estimate depends on good information. Photos of the backyard taken from the back door and from the bottom of the slope help a lot. A copy of your plat or survey helps too, along with any HOA guidelines for your Brentwood neighborhood. Tell us whether the deck and fence are one project or two, and whether you have a date in mind. When you are ready, send the details through the [estimate request form](#estimate) on this page.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval for a deck or fence in Brentwood?
faqs.a: If your home is in a subdivision with covenants, most likely yes. A Brentwood HOA will often want a simple drawing that shows where the project sits on the lot, plus the material and color. Some have written fence standards you can request. Get approval in writing before work starts. Changes a committee asks for after the fact cost far more than waiting for a meeting.

faqs.q: Can a deck or fence go on a steep Brentwood backyard?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Steep ground calls for more planning, not a different answer. A deck on a hillside may need taller posts with extra bracing and a longer stair run, and some footings may have to work around rock. On a slope, a fence gets stepped or racked panels and careful gate placement. Very steep or heavily wooded strips sometimes make more sense left unfenced, and a straight estimate should say so.

faqs.q: Should I build the deck or the fence first?
faqs.a: It depends on what bothers you most right now. If the back door opens onto a drop and there is nowhere to sit outside, the deck usually wins. With a dog that needs room to run, the fence may come first. Many Brentwood owners end up doing both. Planning them together lets the fence tie into the deck stairs or the house in a sensible spot, even if the work happens in separate seasons.

deck.description: Deck builder for Brentwood, TN hillside homes: raised decks on sloped lots, footings in rock and clay, shaded yards, and HOA review.
deck.intro: In Brentwood, the back door often opens onto a drop. Many homes here sit on hillside lots, so the main floor can be well above the yard, with a walkout basement below and hardwoods past the lawn. A deck in that spot carries real load at height, so it has to stand on solid footings and keep people safe near the edge. It also has to look finished enough to get past an architectural committee. This page walks through what a careful Brentwood deck builder plans for before the first post goes in.

sections.heading: Why so many Brentwood decks sit high off the ground
paragraphs: Sloped lots put the yard well below the main floor at the back of the house. A deck built off the kitchen ends up tall, sometimes tall enough to walk under. Height brings its own list of needs. Posts get longer and need bracing so the frame does not rock when people move around. The ledger, where the deck meets the house, has to be flashed so water cannot get behind it and rot the rim joist. Guards and stair rails matter more when a fall would be serious.

Stairs are the part owners tend to underestimate. A long run of steps from a raised deck takes up real yard space, and on a Brentwood hillside the bottom step can land on ground that keeps falling away. Adding a landing partway down often makes the stairs easier to use. Sometimes the better answer is a smaller upper deck with steps down to a second level or a patio at the walkout. Those choices are easier to sort out on paper than after the framing is up.

sections.heading: Footings in limestone and clay
paragraphs: Much of Middle Tennessee sits on limestone, and around Brentwood it can turn up close to the surface in hilly yards. It is common for the auger to stop short in one hole and run clean in the hole beside it. When that happens, the footing is designed for what is actually there instead of forced. The clay above the rock brings a different problem. It holds water and swells when wet, then shrinks in a dry late summer, so footings need to reach stable soil and posts should never stand in a puddle.

Some lots near the Little Harpeth River or the creeks that feed it stay wet for a while after heavy rain. If your yard has a low spot where water gathers, keep posts out of it and make sure the ground under the deck drains away from the house. It is also worth checking whether any part of the lot is in a mapped floodplain, since that can bring extra review from whichever office issues your permit.

sections.heading: Choosing deck boards for a shaded Brentwood yard
paragraphs: Wooded lots are part of why people buy in Brentwood, but trees are hard on a deck. Shade keeps boards damp longer after rain, and damp wood grows mildew and moss faster. Leaves collect in the gaps between boards and hold moisture against the joists. On a pressure treated pine deck, that means cleaning and sealing on a regular schedule. Cedar has some natural resistance to decay but still needs attention in deep shade.

Many owners with shaded lots look at composite decking because it does not need stain, though it still needs washing to keep mildew off the surface. Composite can get hot underfoot in full afternoon sun, which matters less under a tree canopy. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) goes deeper on upkeep and looks. Whatever goes on top, the framing underneath is usually pressure treated lumber, so keeping it dry still matters.

sections.heading: Finish details that matter on a Brentwood deck
paragraphs: Brentwood homeowners tend to expect a deck that looks like it came with the house. That comes down to details. Fascia boards can cover the rim joists and give the frame a clean face. Hidden fasteners keep screw heads off the walking surface. Railing matters most on a raised deck, because you look through it every time you sit down. Slim metal balusters or a thinner top rail can keep a view into the woods open, where a heavy wood railing would block it.

The space under a tall deck needs a plan too. Left open, it collects leaves and slowly turns into storage. Skirting made of boards or lattice closes it off but should leave gaps for air so the framing can dry. If you want that area as a covered patio outside a walkout basement, the drainage between the deck boards has to be decided before the decking goes down. Deciding early costs less than retrofitting later.

sections.heading: Permits and HOA review for a Brentwood deck
paragraphs: A raised or attached deck will usually need a building permit, with inspections along the way. Requirements vary, so check with the codes office that covers your address. That is not always the city. Some homes with a Brentwood mailing address are across the line in Davidson County, which has its own codes office and process. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains in general terms how permits and inspections work.

HOA approval is its own step, and in many Brentwood subdivisions it comes before the permit. Committees in neighborhoods such as Annandale or Governors Club may ask where the deck sits on the lot and what color it will be. A clear drawing with the footprint marked and a short material list makes the review simpler. Build that approval time into your plans, especially if you want the deck finished before a certain season.

sections.heading: What to ask any deck builder before you sign
paragraphs: Whoever you hire, ask how they plan to handle the slope and footings on your lot in particular. A good deck builder should be able to show you where the posts go and explain how the ledger is attached and flashed. Find out who pulls the permit and who handles the HOA submission. It also helps to know what happens if a footing hole hits rock. Clear answers to those questions tell you more than a low number on a page. When you are ready, send your details through our [estimate form](#estimate).

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Brentwood?
faqs.a: Most likely, if the deck is attached to the house or raised off the ground. Requirements vary, so confirm with the codes office that serves your address before work begins. Homes inside Brentwood city limits go through the city, while some homes with a Brentwood mailing address sit in Davidson County and go through a different office. If you have an HOA, its approval is a separate step.

faqs.q: Can a deck go off the main floor when my yard drops a full story?
faqs.a: Yes, and on sloped Brentwood lots that situation is common. A tall deck needs heavier planning than one near the ground. Expect larger posts, bracing to keep the frame from swaying, and a carefully flashed ledger. Stairs will run long, so a landing or a lower level partway down is often worth it. Inspectors may also look more closely at a deck that stands this high.

faqs.q: Is composite or wood better for a shaded Brentwood deck?
faqs.a: Both can work. Under heavy shade, wood stays damp longer and needs more frequent cleaning and sealing to hold off mildew and rot. Composite skips the staining, which is why many owners on wooded lots lean toward it, but it still needs a wash now and then. If part of the deck gets strong afternoon sun, keep in mind that composite runs warmer than wood. Budget and how much upkeep you want usually decide it.

faqs.q: What happens if footing holes hit rock?
faqs.a: It is common in the hills around Brentwood. Sometimes the hole can go deeper with a rock bit or other equipment. Other times the footing is adjusted to bear on the rock itself, which can be a strong base when the rock is sound. The right approach depends on the plans and what your inspector will accept. Your deck builder should explain how they will handle rock before the job starts, since it can change the schedule and the cost.

faqs.q: Can I replace an old Brentwood deck with a bigger one?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but a bigger footprint raises new questions. Your HOA may want to review the new size and placement even though a deck was already there. The codes office will likely treat it as new work, so old footings and the old ledger may not be reusable. It is also a good time to check the siding and rim joist behind the old ledger for rot, since that damage tends to hide until the old deck comes off.

fence.description: Fence installation in Brentwood, TN for sloped, wooded lots: stepped privacy fence lines, gates that clear the grade, HOA review, and survey checks.
fence.intro: Fence installation in Brentwood usually starts with two questions: how much of the yard to fence, and how to get the fence down the hill. Many lots here are large and wooded, and the backyard often falls away from the house toward the rear line. In many established subdivisions, an architectural committee also reviews fence style and color. This page covers what a Brentwood fence company should think through with you, from rocky post holes to the approvals that come before them.

sections.heading: Stepped and racked fences on Brentwood slopes
paragraphs: There are two ways to run a fence down a hill. A stepped fence keeps each panel level and drops it at every post, like a staircase. It looks tidy and suits board on board or horizontal styles, but it leaves triangle shaped gaps under the low end of each panel. A racked fence tilts the panels to follow the ground, so the bottom stays close to the grass. Racking suits a steady slope, while stepping handles sharp changes in grade better. Some panel styles, including many vinyl panels, can only rack a little.

On a Brentwood lot with a dog, those gaps under a stepped fence matter. A small dog can slip through one, and a bigger dog may dig at any gap it can reach. Closing them takes a bottom board cut to the grade. Gates need extra thought on a slope as well. A gate that swings downhill clears the ground, while one swinging uphill may drag. Our guide on [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) goes into post spacing and drainage too.

sections.heading: Wooded lot lines and rocky post holes
paragraphs: Many Brentwood backyards end at a tree line, and the property line often runs right through it. A fence can jog around a large trunk, but it should never be nailed or screwed to a tree. Roots near the surface make post holes harder to place, and cutting big roots can hurt the tree. Before clearing a path, ask whether your HOA or the city has rules about removing larger trees. Along a shaded wooded line, a wood fence will stay damp longer and need more upkeep.

Limestone lies under much of the Brentwood area, sometimes just below the roots. Rock can turn up in some post holes and not others along the same line. That slows the work and can mean shifting a post slightly or drilling. The clay above the rock holds water around the base of a post, so the concrete should be shaped to shed water away from the wood. Before fence installation starts, someone has to call Tennessee 811 so buried utility lines get marked. State law requires that call before digging.

sections.heading: Deciding how much of a big lot to fence
paragraphs: On a larger Brentwood lot, fencing the whole boundary can mean a long run through woods and over steep ground nobody uses. Many owners fence the flatter part of the yard near the house instead and leave the back section open. That shortens the run and keeps the fence where you can see it and look after it. It still gives a dog or kids a safe space. The fence can tie into the corners of the house or into a deck, so plan those connections with any deck work you have coming.

Think about gates before you settle the layout. If you mow the lower yard, you will want a gate wide enough for a riding mower, plus one near the driveway or trash cans for daily use. Where you can, put gates on the flattest stretch of the fence line so they swing freely. If there is a pool, barrier rules are stricter than for a regular yard fence, so confirm them with the codes office before you choose a design.

sections.heading: Privacy fence styles that fit Brentwood HOA rules
paragraphs: A privacy fence makes the most sense where a neighbor's house or a road sits close behind you. In a Brentwood subdivision, the committee will likely care about style as much as height. Many covenants require the finished side to face out, and some limit color to natural tones or an approved stain. Board on board and shadowbox styles give solid screening and look finished from both sides. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares these styles in more detail.

Get the covenants and any written fence standards before you pick a style. Some neighborhoods allow taller fences in the backyard and only lower ones toward the front of the house, while others limit solid fences in certain spots. Send the committee a drawing of the fence line along with the material and stain color. Start early if you want the fence up by a certain date, since many committees meet on a set schedule.

sections.heading: Finding the property line on a Brentwood lot
paragraphs: On wooded lots, an old fence or a tree line is not a reliable guide to where your property ends. A survey or pinned corners should come first, especially on the long, irregular lines that bigger lots often have. Many owners set the fence slightly inside the line so they can maintain both sides without stepping onto a neighbor's land. Talk with the neighbor anyway before the posts go in. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) covers surveys and neighbor conversations.

Permit rules for fences vary. Check with whichever office issues permits for your street, which may be the City of Brentwood or, for some Brentwood addresses, an office in Davidson County. Look at your plat for easements as well. Utility and drainage easements often run along rear lot lines, and a fence built across one may have to come out if a utility needs access.

sections.heading: Choosing a fence company for a Brentwood yard
paragraphs: Whether you live in Concord Crossing or on a street with no HOA at all, get estimates that describe the same fence so you can compare them fairly. Each one should name the style and material and list every gate with its width. It should also explain how the posts are set and how the fence handles the slope. Ask each fence company how they plan to deal with rock and whether hauling away an old fence is included. Clear written answers matter more than the lowest number. When you are ready, send us the details through the [estimate form](#estimate), along with a few photos of the slope.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in Brentwood?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live and what you are building. Rules can differ between the City of Brentwood and Davidson County, where some Brentwood addresses sit, and pool barriers usually carry their own requirements. Ask the office that handles building permits for your address before any work starts. If you live in a subdivision, HOA approval is a separate step, and its rules on style and height may be tighter than the city's.

faqs.q: How does a privacy fence go up on a steep Brentwood backyard?
faqs.a: On a steep yard the panels are usually stepped, so each section stays level and drops at the post. That leaves gaps at the low corners, which a bottom board cut to the grade can close. On a gentler, even slope, racked panels that follow the ground often look cleaner. Post spacing and gate placement both change on a hill, so the layout should be marked on site instead of planned from a plat alone.

faqs.q: Can a fence go around trees on my Brentwood property line?
faqs.a: Yes. The fence can jog around a trunk or stop short with a return, and posts can shift to miss the biggest roots. Attaching boards to a tree is a bad idea, since the trunk keeps growing and pushes the fence out of line. If the tree sits right on the line, talk with your neighbor first, because it may be partly theirs.

faqs.q: What kind of fence works for dogs on a large Brentwood lot?
faqs.a: For most dogs, a solid fence tall enough that they cannot easily see over it works well, as long as the bottom stays close to the ground. Stepped sections on a slope need their gaps closed. Dogs that dig may need wire buried along the base. Gates should close and latch on their own. Fencing a smaller area near the house is often more practical than the full boundary, and it is easier to walk and check.

faqs.q: Which side of the fence should face my neighbor?
faqs.a: In many Brentwood subdivisions the covenants require the finished side to face out, toward the neighbor or the street. Even where no rule says so, it is the usual courtesy. Board on board and shadowbox styles sidestep the question because they look finished from both sides. Check your HOA documents before choosing, since a committee can send a submission back if the wrong side faces out.
